title: Stablecoin Issuers’ Growing Appetite for Treasury Securities - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed finds stablecoin issuers (Tether, USDC) added about $200B of Treasuries in five years, over 40% of China's holdings decline, and outbought Japan in short-term Treasuries since 2023. Trend extrapolation implies about $400B by 2030, still small relative to US financing needs.

insights.claim: The share of US Treasury securities held by foreigners has fallen from a peak above 50% around 2008 to roughly 30% in early 2026, even as federal debt held by the public rose from about 35% of GDP in 2006 to roughly 100%.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Structural loss of the marginal foreign buyer raises the question of who funds rising deficits and at what term premium; watch the TIC and Fed Z.1 holder shares.

insights.claim: Foreign governments' share of foreign Treasury holdings fell from nearly 100% in the 1970s to just above 40% by early 2026, so private foreign investors now dominate foreign demand.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: A more private, price-sensitive foreign base means Treasury demand is more rate-elastic than the reserve-manager era.

insights.claim: China's Treasury holdings have fallen by more than half since their late-2013 peak, with the often-cited driver being Beijing's desire to diversify reserves across a broader range of global assets.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: China's diversification is a persistent headwind for long-end Treasury demand; monitor SAFE/TIC data for further declines.

insights.claim: If the Treasury investor base shifts toward private investors who are more sensitive to global interest rates, then any perception that US debt is riskier could make them demand greater compensation, eroding the so-called exorbitant privilege of low-cost financing.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Risk premium on Treasuries becomes more reactive to fiscal-credibility shocks; supports term-premium-up scenarios.
insights.quote: Hence, if U.S. debt were perceived as riskier, the larger share of private investors could start requiring greater compensation to hold Treasury securities.

insights.claim: Stablecoin issuers have become a novel source of Treasury demand because, to protect one-to-one dollar convertibility, they hold liquid assets, particularly short-term Treasury securities.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth translates mechanically into T-bill demand; crypto adoption is now a rates-market variable.

insights.claim: Tether and USD Coin make up more than 80% of stablecoin market capitalization as of mid-August 2026, and their issuers hold a large fraction of assets in short-term Treasuries alongside cash, bank deposits and repurchase agreements.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Treasury demand from stablecoins is concentrated in two issuers, so issuer-specific reserve decisions or regulation can move bill demand.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: The two largest stablecoin issuers' Treasury holdings have grown more than tenfold over five years, largely surpassing growth in Treasury bill holdings of foreign governments.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuers now rival sovereigns as a bill-market marginal buyer.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: Over five years stablecoin issuers added about $200 billion of Treasury holdings, more than 40% of the decline in China's holdings, partially offsetting Chinese diversification.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: A partial substitution of Chinese selling by crypto-dollar demand; net effect on yields depends on maturity mix.
insights.quote: Over the past five years, stablecoin issuers have increased their Treasury security holdings by about $200 billion, that is, more than 40% of the decline in China’s holdings over the same period.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: China's decline in Treasury holdings is mostly in longer-term debt, while stablecoin issuers are buying short-term securities, so the offset is a maturity mismatch that supports bills more than the long end.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Stablecoin demand compresses front-end yields but does not backstop duration; a curve-steepening implication.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: Since 2023 stablecoin issuers have increased holdings of short-term Treasuries by more than Japan, the largest non-US holder, which drove the recent pickup in foreign official bill demand.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Stablecoins have outgrown the biggest foreign holder as incremental bill buyers.
insights.quote: Notably, since 2023, stablecoin issuers have increased their holdings of short-term Treasury securities more than Japan.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: Some research cited by the authors finds stablecoin issuers' Treasury demand is already large enough to have a measurable impact on short-term government bond yields.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Stablecoin flows may be a tradeable driver of bill yields; watch stablecoin supply changes against front-end pricing.

insights.claim: Stablecoin issuers can inherit the problems of fixed exchange rate regimes and banks: if holders doubt par redemption, runs can occur, which is why issuers hold historically safe and liquid assets.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: A stablecoin run would force rapid liquidation of Treasury bills, a channel for stress in short-term funding markets.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act of 2025 will require approved domestic stablecoin issuers to back issuance one-to-one with high-quality liquid assets such as Treasury bills, locking in structural bill demand tied to stablecoin growth.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Regulation converts stablecoin growth into a legally required T-bill bid; regulatory changes abroad are a swing factor.
insights.locator: Stablecoin issuers' demand for Treasury securities

insights.claim: Extrapolating recent trend growth, stablecoin issuers' Treasury demand could nearly double to roughly $400 billion by the end of 2030, and other studies project even stronger growth.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Base case of about $400B is a useful sizing anchor for stablecoin-linked bill demand; upside cases exist.
insights.quote: the associated demand for short-term Treasury securities would nearly double to about $400 billion by the end of 2030

insights.claim: Even at $400 billion, stablecoin Treasury holdings would stay substantially smaller than US government financing needs, so they are a meaningful but not decisive source of demand.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Do not overstate stablecoins as a solution to deficit financing; they are a marginal bill buyer.

insights.claim: The projection is highly uncertain: stablecoin growth depends on regulations worldwide, competing products, and possible bank technologies that ease cross-border digital payments and compete with stablecoins.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Bank-issued tokens or tighter rules are the main risks to the stablecoin Treasury-demand story.

insights.claim: Stablecoin use is higher relative to GDP in Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, mostly in international transactions, likely lowering cross-border and remittance costs and offering a store of value where local currency is volatile.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Emerging-market dollarization via stablecoins is the demand base behind issuer reserves; a source of structural dollar demand.

insights.claim: Whether stablecoin demand is additive depends on the investor mix: stablecoins could attract new investors who do not hold Treasuries, or merely let existing holders hold Treasuries indirectly.
insights.speaker: Aleisha Sawyer
insights.so_what: Net new demand versus repackaged demand determines whether stablecoins lower yields overall.
